text: Bay Ganyo, having finally convinced himself that there was no possibility of lodging at Jireček’s, picked up his saddlebags, ignoring the host’s entreaties to leave them at his home until he found a place, and set off, accompanied by the servant, for the Nàrodny Kavàrna — the café where the Bulgarian students gathered. It was already seven o’clock when he entered the café with the saddlebags in hand and the kalpak on his head. Just try not to recognize who he was and where he came from! To the left of the entrance, around a table, sat several Bulgarian students.

One of them saw the entering compatriot and nudged the others: "A Bulgarian, a Bulgarian!" Everyone turned at the moment when Bay Ganyo stopped a waiter carrying a tray of coffees and, trying as much as possible to mangle the Bulgarian words to make them intelligible to the foreigner, asked in a loud voice: "Where here Bulgarian boys?" — accompanying the question with a movement of his head and his free hand. A collective laugh from the left side ended the waiter's bewilderment. Bay Ganyo turned and recognized his dark-eyed, dark-haired, huddled compatriots.

— Oh! Good day! So this is where you were? — he cried out heartily, set down his saddlebags, and began grabbing the students' hands. — Why are you staring at me? Don't be afraid, I'm Bulgarian... Come on, make some room for me to sit down.
— What is your name, sir? — one of the students asked curiously.
— Me? Why do you ask? Ganyo Balkanski. I’ve brought some rose oil to your Prague — here it is, right here in the saddlebags.
— Is that so? — cried one of the younger students in patriotic ecstasy. — Let’s see it.
He really had only heard of rose oil.

— What is there to look at, it’s just oil like any other — answered Bay Ganyo, — it’s not for you. Forget about the oil and tell me something else: where can I stay? I’ve just been at Bay Jireček’s...
— Is that so? — the exalted student cried out again.

— What do you mean "is that so"? Why shouldn't I have gone to see him? I went—thinking he’d show some decency, invite me over to his place. Such faith! My apartment is cramped, says he, and I don’t know what else, and this and that. He loved Bulgarians, says he... Him! When there’s a profit in it, even your Uncle Ganyo knows how to love. — Is that how you welcome a Bulgarian? A Bulgarian!... To tell you the truth, the man did feed me. And what food it was—anyway, never mind that!... Bulgarians are far more hospitable; a Bulgarian, even if he has only one room, he’ll still invite you in...

Some of the students began to realize what Bay Ganyo was driving at and were waiting from minute to minute for him to show his hand. Only the exalted student reacted sympathetically to his words and openly shared his indignation at the inhospitality of the foreigners.
— "Indeed, our Bulgarians are very hospitable," he confirmed with the utmost confidence, "the locals here don't want to know you. We just hang around these cafes..."

The student who said those words was very advanced in civilization, but for some reason, he did not enjoy a particularly good reputation among his comrades; it seemed that certain sins weighed upon his soul; it was said, among other things, that he was very fond of "striking a bargain." And no wonder! This wretched sin—avarice—by the contagion of the surrounding domestic environment, takes root almost from childhood; it withers the soul of the young man, turning him into the coldest of egoists: nothing tender, nothing noble remains in him. Material interest governs all the actions of the miser and determines his relations with those around him: no moral impulse precedes, and no remorse follows his actions, which are directed toward obtaining profit without any regard for the means. Even when these actions bring disaster or disgrace upon someone, even then, instead of remorse, the miserly egoist feels satisfaction, as if the loss of others were his gain, and the misfortune of others his happiness. Only one thing would trouble our young egoist—to be outsmarted by someone. While among other nations the word "cunning" is synonymous with being devious or treacherous, and when attached to a person would lower them in the estimation of society, here the epithet "cunning" is worn like the most honorable of decorations: "My! What a cunning lad he turned out to be; long life to his father, he fooled us all! We couldn't trick him! Well done! Bravo!"

No actions or relationships had any meaning for Bodkov—that was his name—unless they resulted in some "freebie," some easy profit. (Are there words in European languages corresponding to these, in this particular sense?) If he visited the local families, he did not do so out of sociability or a desire to become acquainted with the lifestyle of more civilized circles; the intellectual and moral interests of that society not only failed to engage him but were a burden to him—they were like boring intervals, intolerable pauses that separated him from the goal of his visits—from the "freebie": be it a little feast or an outing at their expense. He could not imagine an acquaintance with women without ulterior motives. He kept a whole list of maidens—how much dowry each had; nothing else interested him in that regard. Likewise, self-interest determined his relationships with his comrades. Flattery, slander, petty intrigues, and denunciations were the tools of his personal gain. Even things such as national and tribal sympathies and antipathies served him only as a means to extract personal profit. More than once he had dipped into the purses of various Slavic committees, posing now as a survivor "from Batak," now as an "emigrant." But in these matters, Aslanov was the greater master.

Such was the exalted student who supported Bay Ganyo in his opinion regarding the hospitality of foreigners.
— Yes, we just languish here in the cafes, no one invites us over — he repeated, to please Bay Ganyo.
— What are you so fired up about? Is this the time to be picking a fight — one of the students spoke up — when we have a guest?

— Let the man talk a bit, he’s not asking for money, is he? — Bay Ganyo reassured him with this typical argument: “H e   i s n ’ t   a s k i n g   f o r   m o n e y,   i s   h e!” He can say whatever he wants, do whatever he wants, as long as he doesn’t ask for money, as long as he doesn’t touch our pocket, our interests. He can even lie, he’s not asking for money!

But after this chance incident, it was no longer possible to maintain a convivial conversation. The group fell silent, and one by one, they began to disperse. Of the Bulgarians, only Bai Ganyo and the over-excited student remained; the latter did not want to miss the opportunity to derive some benefit from his chance encounter with the Bulgarian rose oil merchant. — The pot rolled over and found its lid.

Not an hour had passed, and the student managed to slander his comrades before Bay Ganyo so thoroughly that he made him cry out from the bottom of his heart: “Bravo, you rascals!” After another hour, Bay Ganyo was already in the student’s room, who had managed quite skillfully to exploit the guest’s arrival for his own benefit, recommending him to his landlords as his relative, a millionaire who “owns a multitude of rose oil factories.” He managed to borrow ten guilders from the landlady—to whom he had not paid the room rent for quite a long time. While in one room the student was extolling Bay Ganyo’s riches, in the adjoining room Bay Ganyo had already stripped off his *anteriya* and was searching for something in it with great attention, muttering under his breath: “That cursed vermin has bred again.” The concept of cleanliness is not developed to a very high degree in Bay Ganyo. “Can a living soul ever be without vermin?” say the old folk in our country, and comforted by this axiom, they do not hinder the reproduction of the little creatures too zealously. And why should they deprive themselves of such a pleasure: the sun has come out, and what is the use of that sun if one cannot go out onto the veranda, stretch out on the mat, sneeze two or three times from its dust, and have his grandmother come, and lay his head on her knee, and she sticks her bony fingers with mourning nails into his hair and, as if she were sorting rice, starts *click!*—here, *click!*—there, and when the little creatures get frightened and scurry over his head, and there is a pleasant tickling, and the grandmother starts singing, and that Balkan sun of yours is shining! An idyll...

Bay Ganyo, after finishing his entomological searches, restored his attire and, without knocking, entered the adjacent room, but instantly cried out: "Pardon!" — and with good reason: he found the student and the landlady's daughter in a most tender *vis-à-vis* — they were embracing, as befits two young hearts in love. The girl, shamed, fled into the other room.
— Hey, why are you coming in like that? You've embarrassed the girl — the student said with an ironic wink.
— You’ve hit the jackpot! — Bay Ganyo whispered mysteriously, his eyes gleaming like a monastery tomcat’s. — A sleek one, devil take her! Is she a maid?
— What a servant! The landlady's daughter!

— Is that so? You can't tell them apart here—who's the maid and who's the mistress; they’re all so polished, all dressed so cleanly. One comes across you, grinning all oily-like; you think she’s a maid, you accost her, and you bring trouble on your head. Another one comes along, pretty and modest; you think, "Aha, this is the mistress," you stand up for her, invite her to sit down, she acts all shy—naturally!—you speak to her with great ceremony, and then later you see her cleaning your boots!

From the student’s accounts, accompanied by various gestures with which he embellished and lent more force and significance to his words, Bay Ganyo learned that for several months, under the guise of pure love, the young man had been assailing the daughter of his widowed landlady with irresistible persistence.

— And she, the silly thing — the narrator explains — hopes that I’ll take her as my wife! Let her hope, and let her feed me well, let her sew shirts for me. If she were some rich girl — I could understand a man marrying her — but she’s a pauper just like me. She hangs around me because she thinks I’m a rich man. If she only knew what I really am, would she be so greedy? The local women here are terrible schemers! But I know how to play them, don’t I? — And he went on at great length about how he plays them...
— Bravo! — cried Bay Ganyo with oily eyes, delighted by his young interlocutor.

— Wait a minute, is that all? If that's it, it's nothing! There's another one, another one I've got my eye on, but who knows! Now, if I could just turn her head—there’s a real prize to be had there. She's rich! I'm invited to their place tomorrow; they're taking me on an outing to a village.
— And when are you going to take me to the factories? — asked the practical Bay Ganyo.

— Easy enough, the day after tomorrow. You stay here tomorrow, hang around them; when they see you don't know the language, they won't let you go to the inn, they'll invite you to their place and you'll get a free meal.

And indeed, early the next morning, the student went out visiting, while Bay Ganyo remained in the lodgings alone with the hosts. As usual, on this day too, he rose very early, woke and saw off his companion, and waited for a whole hour more until the landladies woke up. This waiting was very difficult for him; he felt a certain great need, like any human being, but had forgotten to ask the student where *that place* was, and—willy-nilly—he had to wait for the household to get up and—shame or no shame—ask them. It is a very bad thing when one does not know the language in a foreign land; they cannot understand you even for the simplest thing, and you must always explain with your hands and fingers, showing them... But then, can everything be shown? Bay Ganyo knew languages: he could speak Turkish to you like a Turk, he understood Vlach, Serbian, and Russian every now and then, but the Germans and Czechs did not understand a single one of these languages. It could not be said that Bay Ganyo knew no German at all; he knew a word or two.

In the next room, the hostesses got up and began to stir. Bay Ganyo peered through the keyhole, not out of any indecent curiosity, but to see if they were already dressed; and carefully, with bated breath, as he familiarized himself with their toilette, he was composing a phrase in German in his mind that would correspond to our: “Where is that thing, for the big business?” — and finally, from a literal translation, he cobbled together the phrase: “Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit?” — Knock! knock! knock!
— Come in! — two female voices called out from the next room.
Bay Ganyo opened the door, said a "pardon," and shyly uttered: — Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit? — and wiggled his fingers to emphasize the question.
— Co, pan? — the girl asked in bewilderment, trying to examine the appearance of the millionaire recommended by her lover.
— Fur gross Arbeit? — repeated Bay Ganyo, even more abashed, and again gestured with his fingers and head, but he noticed that they did not understand him.
They understood him, but not as they should have; the women thought he was informing them that he had come to do great things, a major trade in rose oil.

"The devil!" thought Bay Ganyo. "What am I to do now?" And so that at least the daughter would not be a witness to his awkward predicament, he beckoned the mother into his room, closed the door, and after repeating the question in German once more, he supplemented it this time with a desperate gesture, which caused the lady to flee into the other room, choking with suppressed laughter. The maid appeared and satisfied Bay Ganyo’s curiosity. A trio of continuous female laughter shook the walls.
The aroma wafting through the open kitchen doors into the hallway whetted Bai Ganyo’s appetite, and out of curiosity, he peeked in to see what was cooking. The landlady and the maid were there.

— Was ist das? — asked Bay Ganyo in a condescending tone, not so much out of a desire to acquaint himself with the culinary arts of the Czechs as to show that he had been around Europe and knew these things, and that he could speak German as well. — Soup, right? You're cooking soup? I know. Ich versten supa!

And Bai Ganyo, using a mixture of German, Bulgarian, and distorted Bulgarian, aided by impressive gesticulations, let the landlady understand that he would not mind sampling their cuisine. Seeing that the women showed a greater inclination to express themselves in Czech, Bai Ganyo also switched to "Czech" and supported his condescending desire with the words: "ya hochem kushay," interpreting these words by repeatedly touching his fingers to his open mouth; then, holding up three fingers, he poked his chest with his index finger, poked the same finger toward the landlady's chest, and a third time pointed into the air, as if indicating the landlady's invisible daughter—meaning, "to eat together, all three of us!" It was also important for Bai Ganyo to know at what time he would be lunching, as he intended to go for a walk and didn't want to miss the meal and then "have to pay for food when there's a freebie to be had"; so he pulled out his enormous watch and, thrusting it under the landlady's nose, made her point to the hands to show him when he would "kushay." Once satisfied that everything was settled, Bai Ganyo went into his room, stuffed the vials into his sash, and headed out for a stroll—partly for the walk itself, and partly on the off chance he might run into a customer for his rose oil.

Bai Ganyo saw that many streets intersected, that one could easily take the wrong path or get lost, and being a practical man, he looked around for some sign by which he might recognize the house. On the opposite side, on a back wall, he saw an inscription in large letters; he pulled out his notebook, licked his pencil, wrote down an exact copy of the inscription, and, fully confident that he held the most precise address of his lodgings in his hands, he set off through the narrow streets of old Prague. Now he’d look at this, now he’d look at that, here a customer, there a customer—he got carried away, and not only did he get carried away, but he lost his way. Now what? When he started searching for his house, he got even more bogged down in the Jewish streets; an hour passed, two hours passed, he hit a dead end in some building—no way out; he tried another direction, walked and walked, and popped out on the banks of the Vltava. "Damn it all, now what?" And to top it off, lunchtime came; it came and it went. That dear Bai Ganyo of ours, with his sleeves tucked up, trudged and trudged, becoming soaked with sweat, panting, looking like a total sight. The people he encountered, especially the policemen, looked at him suspiciously: this unsettled him even more. "Damn it all, now what?" And he was hungry, a revolution was brewing in his stomach, but why the devil should he throw his money to the wind when he had been invited to lunch?

But, you might say, why does Bai Ganyo wander the streets when the address is in his pocket? Well, that’s just the point! And Bai Ganyo is no fool; do you really think it didn’t occur to him to take out his notebook, stop this person or that on the street, and, pointing to the written address, ask with his fingers “which way”? He knows how these things are done; he stops both men and women, but a strange thing happens—whoever he stops to ask, as soon as he shows them what is written, they either look at him in amazement and burst out laughing, or turn away from him with indignation. One lady, likely some nervous old maid, when he showed her the address, snapped at him so sharply that even Bai Ganyo lost his nerve. “The devil take it, either I’m crazy or all of Prague has gone mad,” he thinks to himself, unable to fathom the effect his written address produces; and as he ponders, he looks around and suddenly—isn’t that a stroke of luck?—he sees rising before him the *Nàrodny Kavàrna*, the café where the Bulgarian students gather. Bai Ganyo goes inside and finds the angry student.
— Good day! Tell me, my good man, am I crazy, or are the people here crazy? — asks Bay Ganyo, out of breath, with wet hair plastered to his forehead.
The student looked at him questioningly. Bay Ganyo told him how he had lost his way, how he had inquired about his lodgings using the address, and what they had told him in response.
The student, knowing that the Czechs—rude and fanatical only toward the Germans, but otherwise quite courteous—could not help but wonder how it was that they would not do a favor for Bai Ganyo.
— Read, please, what is written here! — and Bay Ganyo held out the little notebook.
The student read it:, at first he frowned slightly, then he burst out laughing!...
— Did you show this address to any lady? — he asked through his laughter.
— Why? I showed it, after all! Well?
— Well? Do you know what is written here?
— What?
— It is written "...Zde je zapovedeno..." "It is forbidden here to..." You copied it from some wall.
— Well, I'll be! Look at that! Tsk... tsk... tsk! Are you telling the truth? Look at that! — said Bay Ganyo, clicked his tongue a little, and then he too began to laugh.

The student did not know Bodkov’s lodgings—they were not on visiting terms—and so he advised Bai Ganyo to wait, for some Bulgarian or other would surely come along to show him the house. It is easy to say “wait,” but let’s see if Bai Ganyo’s stomach was of the same opinion! And that it was not of the same opinion, it proved demonstratively with an endless rumbling.
— Are you hungry? — the student asked him, hearing the revolutionary signals.

— Who, me? I'm not — Bai Ganyo lied slightly, because if he told the truth, the other would show him the inn, and it wouldn't do at all to admit to him ("How could I tell such a stubborn brat!") that a free meal awaited him at the hostesses' place.

A conversation between Bay Ganyo and the "stubborn kid" failed to take root. From their very first meeting, they instinctively sensed that they were not meant for each other, for according to the Bulgarian proverb (oh, what exquisite proverbs the Bulgarian genius has created!) “scabby donkeys can smell each other from nine hills away.” One had just arrived from Bulgaria, the other had been living in Europe; surely they would have had something to talk about, since there must be at least some small difference between the West and our fatherland.

In fact, Bay Ganyo did not notice this difference—and how could he! Wherever he goes, he carries his own atmosphere, his own manners and customs; he seeks out lodgings that suit his tastes and meets only his own kind of people, to whom he is accustomed and in whom, naturally, he sees nothing new. If he goes to Vienna, he will stay at the Hotel London, where it is just as stifling and smells just as much of the kitchen and hydrogen sulfide as it does back home; there he meets the same Turks, Armenians, Serbs, and Arnauts he is used to seeing every day. He won't go to the Café Habsburg for fear of being fleeced; instead, he will duck into the Greek café, which is just as filthy and choked with eternal smoke as our own coffeehouses. If he goes for business, he seeks out Bulgarian merchants, and through them, he doesn't even realize he is coming into contact with Europeans.

As for the fact that European life begins precisely outside this narrow sphere, he neither knows it nor, it seems, does he even care to know. The upbringing, the moral world of the European, his domestic environment—the fruit of centuries of tradition and the gradual refinement of intellectual thought—social struggles and the manner in which they are conducted, museums, libraries, philanthropic institutions, the fine arts, and the thousands of manifestations of progress do not weigh upon Bay Ganyo’s attention.

"As if my father was always listening to operas," Bay Ganyo would say, and charmed by this principle of fossilization and ultra-retrogradism, he is not overly startled by the "new fashion," i.e., by civilization. Yet, for all that, Bay Ganyo lacks the valor of the Chinese—to wall himself in against the invasion of civilization—and despite being inspired by the principle "my father didn't do this, and neither will I," you'll suddenly see that he's put on a clean shirt, donned gloves, and when pressed, he even puts on a frock coat; he grumbles, he laughs, but he puts on the frock coat. You hear him saying "pardon," talking about the "constentution," boasting here and there that he loves "soup," when in fact he would prefer a spicy *chorba* over all European dishes.
— Ah, here comes a Bulgarian boy; he knows Bodkov's lodgings — declared the "stubborn kid"...

— "Come on, take me home," Bay Ganyo turned to the Bulgarian youth with a tone that should have vanished even from our treatment of lazy servants; but the words "politeness" and "courtesy" are newly stolen from the Russian language, "delicacy" is borrowed from the French, and in our country, the most suitable term for these concepts is the word "slobbering." Those soft, gentle, heartfelt forms of address that characterize the relations of civilized people and make life milder and more pleasant are incomprehensible to Bay Ganyo; he speaks as God gave him: "Come on, hey, listen here, take me home." And what is the meaning of: "I beg of you, have the kindness, be so kind"—what is all this slobbering!...

The young Bulgarian led Bay Ganyo to the gate of his lodgings and returned. Bay Ganyo looked at the wretched inscription on the opposite wall, shook his head threateningly at it, clicked his tongue, and entered the house. In the corridor, he met no one; he peeked into the kitchen—the fire there was already out, the dishes cleaned and put away. "Tsk, what a pity, I missed the freebie," Bay Ganyo muttered, entered his room, crouched over his saddlebags, took the vials out of his sash and stuffed them inside, pulled out the greasy kashkaval, cut himself a piece of dry bread, and began to stifle the revolution, smacking his lips so appetizingly that even the laziest Swiss cow would have envied him. To stimulate his lymphatic organs, tired from unproductive labor, he sent down his esophagus a chewed-up hot pepper, which made his eyes water and caused him to accompany his smacking with a sniffle. The maid, who was tidying up in the next room, hearing the strange sounds with which Bay Ganyo accompanied his snack, opened the door and peeked into the room: Bay Ganyo shyly shielded the saddlebags with his back, turned his tearful and sweaty face, said "Pardon!", gave a vigorous sniff, and drove the maid away—that is to say, not that he told her to leave, but she hurried to flee, thinking that the millionaire might have received some mournful news.

Bodkov did not return that evening. Towards evening, the hostesses returned; a fire was lit in the kitchen again, and they began preparing dinner. Bai Ganyo already considered himself one of the family—"after all, why stand on ceremony with women," he says—and without any preamble, he enters the kitchen and explains, more with gestures than words, that he had lost his way in the streets and missed lunch, but no matter—he was owed a lunch and would make up for it with a dinner. Bai Ganyo also understands the culinary arts, and not only does he understand them, but any violation of the craft outrages him. For instance, seeing the hostess preparing to put a fresh fish into boiling water, he rose up with all his energy, grabbed her hand, snatched the fish with his other hand, and signaled with hand and head, as if to say: "Stop, don't move, just watch how fish is cooked!" "Salt!" Bai Ganyo commands. They give him salt; he rolls up his sleeves to the elbows of his hairy arms, reaches into the salt cellar with his none-too-delicate fingers, and begins to salt and rub the fish inside and out, even though it was already salted. "Paprika!"—but where would these fools get paprika! "Black pepper!" Bai Ganyo commands, grabs the pepper, and rubs it onto the fish. "A grill!" trumpets the triumphant cook, but here they couldn't understand him despite all his gestures, and he himself glanced around and couldn't spot a grill; but is this an obstacle for Bai Ganyo? He wasn't born yesterday! Taking the tongs, he raked all the fire to the mouth of the oven, let the other dishes rest (it was just as well they were already done), spread the tongs wide, placed the fish on them, and attempted to shove it into the oven, but the door was narrow; the fish caught, slipped, and—splat!—into the fire. "Oh!" cried the hostess. "Nothing, nothing!" Bai Ganyo reassured her, snatched the fish, blew off the stuck coals and ash, and put it back on the "grill." Smoke and the smell of fish filled the entire kitchen. The hostesses were in despair; Bai Ganyo was beaming—he was in his element now. While roasting the fish, blowing on it, and sniffing, stimulated by the appetizing smoke, he used his free hand—greasy from turning the fish—to command them to set the table so his dish wouldn't get cold: "If fresh fish isn't hot—throw it away!" The fish, roasted, its tail and head rolled in ash, was placed on a plate, and under Bai Ganyo’s "gracious" command: "Quickly! Quickly! While it’s hot, bring lemon and wine; without wine, it’s not worth a penny!"—they sat around the table, having sent the maid running for lemon and wine. What could they do! The "millionaire" wasn't going to change his habits for their pleasure, was he! The hostess reached out to cut the fish. "Please, please, please! Heaven forbid!" cried Bai Ganyo, grabbing her hand; then he turned the fish onto its back, pressed it here and there with his two fingers, and it split into two halves. Well, how could one not triumph! The maid brought a lemon; Bai Ganyo sliced it, gripped a half in his whole fist, and squeezed it over the plate with such diligence that even the pulp of the lemon fell onto the fish. What do you think, does Bai Ganyo have an appetite or not? Hardly as much lemon juice flowed into the plate as the saliva Bai Ganyo swallowed. And the wine was brought. Dinner began.

Carlsbad and I know not what other -bad the Aesculapians recommend to those suffering from stomach catarrh. Let them take these sufferers by the ear and seat them at the table before Bay Ganyo, even if their stomachs are more ruined than the streets of Yuchbunar... you shall see what an effect the spectacle will have on them!... Bay Ganyo is eating, boy, he’s not joking; he eats so his ears flap! Every organ of his body is in motion, with his teeth, tongue, and nose leading the way. This is where one realizes the paleness and poverty of language! With what words, what interjections, what punctuation marks, or finally, what musical notes is it possible to depict those smackings, gruntings, snifflings, clatterings, clickings, and suckings that pour from Bay Ganyo like a hailstorm!... Blessed are the hostesses! Not every Czech woman will have the good fortune to enjoy such a spectacle.

They finally finished eating. They moved into the drawing room. Bay Ganyo, red as a peony, kept twirling his mustache, kept belching into his hand, and kept muttering "pardon." They settled into the chairs. Bay Ganyo rolled a cigarette, greasy from his fingers, and began to puff and blow clouds of smoke through his mustache. Is this not the most suitable moment for enjoyment: for music, for songs, for love? The young woman caught the millionaire's mood and asked him if he liked music. Who? Bay Ganyo? Why, if Bay Ganyo doesn't love music, who else will? Who else has been able to inspire such respect in the Gypsies—that is, the musicians—as Bay Ganyo? Just with a wink of his eye, look what happens to those Gypsies! Fire! Fire! Let that violin wail, let that clarinet shriek!
Your figure is a poplar,
on my heart like two stakes.
I'm stitching your dress
You burned my heart...

— Shut up, you Gypsies! I don't want love songs! Play me some drinking music! — Bay Ganyo shouted at them and banged his glass on the table. They start “The Dark Carnation,” Bay Ganyo bangs his glass, they stop. They start “We Want No Wealth” — he bangs his glass again. They switch to “Green Leaf.” “Ha, see that now! E-e-e-e-h! Come, my joy, come!”... — and smash goes the bottle on the ground or through the window... Well, who is the master of these things? And was it just once, or twice? But   t h e s e   w o m e n   how would they know who your Bay Ganyo is! Even if you tell them how many windowpanes you've smashed to music, they can't understand you!...

— I love music! — Bay Ganyo uttered condescendingly. — I love music! — he repeated and shook his head, which in his opinion expressed the sad necessity of listening to a pathetic tinkling of a piano for the sake of the women. “What do you understand of music-making, of a *muhabet*?” — Bay Ganyo thought to himself.
— The gentleman is playing "Bacon", Mother! — the girl announced her discovery.
— "Bacon, indeed," Bay Ganyo spoke up, "how do you know about it?"

Delighted by his success, Bai Ganyo sat down at the stool to play something more serious, now with good reason. And what could be more serious than "The Night is Terrible"? Bai Ganyo began to p l a y, but even he was dissatisfied with the performance. And quite naturally so! "The Night is Terrible" was not made for the piano; the sounds are cut short: you strike the key on "terri-i-i-ble!" and the note breaks off; the accordion is a different matter entirely! When you put your finger on "...ri-i-i-ble..."—press it, damn it all! Let it drone for half an hour, keep pressing, let it swell in waves until your heart's content! But with a piano—plink, plank, it’s all for nothing! Bai Ganyo saw that the effect produced by "The Little Bacon" was beginning to fade; he thought and thought, then decided: "Wait, let me just sing 'The Night is Terrible' to these womenfolk!..." He paused for a moment, wanting to get into a mournful mood in the spirit of the sorrowful song; he gave a deep sigh, cupped his right hand over his ear, half-closed his eyes, and then—how he bellowed!...

„Grandissimo maestro Verdi! You have no, you cannot have enemies! But if, against all expectations, some monster were to appear, he would be Satan himself. God is great, Esimio Maestro! — and all the arrows of the evil spirit are powerless against you! Only one... only one means can the Deceiver use, and the entire musical world will be covered in mourning... We shall pray, and you pray too, Divin Maestro, to the almighty creator, that he may not allow Satan to lead you into the salon where Bay Ganyo is singing “The night is terrible”... And when your most refined hearing is shaken by the wild, inhuman sounds incomprehensible to you, the Evil Spirit shall reveal the terrible truth to you with his satanic laughter: Ha! ha! ha! Verdi! This is a song from your   d i v i n e   “La Traviata”! Ha! ha! ha! ha-a!!...“
— It's late already, gentlemen — said the shy Ilcho, looking at his watch, — midnight! Let's go home, and some other time, God willing, we shall talk of Bai Ganyo again.

— Say, Ilcho, tell me, why do you hate Bulgarian songs so much? — Dravichkata piped up on the way out.

— Who? Me, hate them? I’m sorry, my dear fellow, but you’ve misunderstood me completely. I am capable of admiring, of losing myself, of being entranced to ecstasy by our beautiful, melancholy folk songs—but by the *true* Bulgarian songs, and not those revolting parodies of vulgar foreign tunes that our "Bay Ganyos" deliver to us, distorted beyond recognition with those Gypsy grace notes and throat-wrenching drunken trills and fiorituras... We have songs, but we have no singers. I am ready to embrace my enemy if he sings "Bogdane, bog da te ubie" or "Ya zapretni, Velo mome, beli rakavi" as they should be sung, and to look askance at my friend when I see him admiring "Zelen listets," "Karanfilcheto," and other such Gypsy "delights"...
